Figures 5-15 and 5-16 show the variations in supply and demand of fuels across different U.S. census region. Most biofuel production is concentrated in the West North Central and East North 53 Central regions while diesel demand is in the West South Central. However, the RD production in most regions has the potential to meet 100% of rail diesel demand in those regions except in the Mountain and Pacific divisions) and part of Northeast (New England). There is also variation in RD sources across regions. While RD-HEFA dominates in most regions, RD-gasification accounts for 100% in the Mountain region and, 58% in the Pacific, 25% in the South Atlantic, 16% in the East South Central, 13% in the West South Central and 3% of production in the East North Central). RD from manure is concentrated in the Midwest (about 4% of the region’s RD), while most regions produce at least some RD from sludge. These regional differences in both volume and fuel pathway can affect delivered cost and adoption. Regions with insufficient local production will rely on supply from other regions, increasing logistics costs and potentially slowing uptake. Regional BD production in the BD100 case slightly differs from the RD100 case. In RD100, production in the Mountain, Pacific and New England divisions is primarily from woody biomass and sludge. In BD100, by contrast, BD is produced from soybeans only in the Mountain and New England divisions, with no production in the Pacific. In total, BD output in BD100 is 14% lower than RD output in RD100. To further refine potential corridors for biofuel adoption, we overlaid state-level biofuel production capacity onto our earlier analysis of projected state-level rail ton-miles, as visualized in Figure 5- 17. This builds upon the -regional supply and demand analyses (Section 5.2.4) is important to note that the precise locations of refueling depots within each state, as well as the accessibility of fuel to rail operators via existing infrastructure, are currently unknown. Therefore, although this overlay analysis offers a valuable starting point, further investigation into refueling depot locations and fuel accessibility at a more granular level is needed to fully assess the feasibility of biofuel implementation on specific rail routes. Rail is especially critical for moving bulk BD and high‑level BD blends, which cannot be transported via regular petroleum pipelines. (EIA, 2024). Rail can provide a feasible means of transportation to move BD and RD from the high-producing states in Figure 5-17 to the states with low/no biofuel production but high state- level rail ton-miles.
